structure.title: Preface and Section I · Ordinary praise under pressure
structure.text: Kant starts with a good will and asks why certain actions deserve moral esteem. A shopkeeper can charge everyone fairly because honesty is profitable. From the customer's side of the counter everything looks exactly right.

structure.title: Section II · Give the reason a form
structure.text: Kant distinguishes commands that depend on an aim from a command that binds anyone capable of acting for reasons. Promising, refusing aid and neglecting a talent give several formulations of the moral law cases to work on.

structure.title: Section III · Why should a rational will be bound?
structure.text: The final move connects the idea of freedom with a will subject to a law it gives itself. The difficulty is explaining why somebody who experiences a world of causes can regard an obligation as genuinely addressed to them.

people.name: A maxim
people.role: The principle on which someone proposes to act
people.text: To examine a false promise Kant needs the intended deception and its purpose. A bare description such as uttering certain words leaves out precisely the policy that is to be tested as a possible universal law.

people.name: Humanity as an end
people.role: A constraint on using another person's agency
people.text: In a deceptive promise the listener appears to agree but lacks the information that would make agreement meaningful. Kant's example puts flesh on the word merely in the prohibition on treating people merely as means.

context.title: Duty and inclination can point the same way
context.text: A kindly impulse may produce a welcome act. Kant wants to isolate what gives the action moral worth, which is why his comparisons often remove the pleasure or personal advantage an agent could have found in doing it.

notice.text: Track what changes while the deed stays the same.
notice.why: Two people can perform the same service and act for quite different reasons. Comparing them puts the burden of Kant's argument on the will, where a spectator cannot simply inspect the evidence.

notice.text: Distinguish two ways a rule can fail.
notice.why: A universal practice of false promising undermines the very institution the promise needs. Other proposed rules describe an imaginable world in which the agent could scarcely will to live. The tests ask different things.

opening: You need money and know nobody will lend it unless you promise to repay. You also know you cannot keep the promise. Kant takes this ordinary temptation seriously enough to ask what a promise would become if everyone treated it that way. His search for morality's foundation strips away reputation, convenience, and the hope of reward. It leads to a demanding account of freedom in which another person's humanity places limits on what you may do, even for a result you badly want.
